summary: The charter correctly identifies the engineer-trust + Fluent-parity gap and articulates a defensible AI-advisor-only contract with concrete grep-able stays/deprecates/reframes tables. However, it does not reconcile the new M1-M6 numbering with the existing ROADMAP.md M1-M4 (Workbench Closed-Loop, COMPLETE) and queued M5-M8 (Beginner Full Stack) sequence, leaves an internal contradiction between §2 Principle B and §3 reframe of the envelope endpoint, and proposes a brittle grep-based contract test as the load-bearing enforcement of the hard contract. None block strategic intent; all should be fixed before status=Accepted.

findings.title: M1-M6 numbering collides with existing ROADMAP.md M1-M4 / M5-M8 without reconciliation
findings.position: §4 (Phased roadmap M1-M6) and frontmatter parent_artifacts ROADMAP.md
findings.problem: ROADMAP.md currently defines two distinct M-sequences: (a) Workbench Closed-Loop M1-M4 (COMPLETE, real-OpenFOAM-LDC dogfood arc) and (b) Beginner Full Stack M5-M8 (queued, with binding gates including M5.1 trust-core micro-PR / M6.0.1 calibration / M7 Path-A first-customer recruitment / M5-M8 stranger-dogfood completion gate). This DEC introduces a third, semantically different M1-M6 (workbench-parity build-out) but only refers obliquely to 'replace the Phase A→B→C→D→E→F→G arc'. The fate of the binding M5-M8 commitments (stranger dogfood, Path-A recruitment, TrustGate hard-cap on imported cases) is unstated. M1.3 'ROADMAP rewrite' is named but its scope (only Phase A-G replacement, or full M5-M8 supersession?) is not specified.
findings.recommendation: Add a §3.5 'Relationship to existing M-sequences' table that names every M-token currently in ROADMAP.md and states explicitly: KEPT (and renumbered to what?) / SUPERSEDED (and on what evidence?) / DEFERRED (and to what trigger?). Particularly call out: M5-M8 stranger-dogfood gate, M5.1 trust-core micro-PR, M6.0.1 calibration unlock, M7 Path-A recruitment prerequisite. If those are folded into the new M1-M6, identify which sub-DEC carries each commitment forward.

findings.title: §2 Principle B (hard contract) contradicts §3 envelope reframe
findings.problem: §2 Principle B states: 'AI code paths (LLM tool dispatch, ai-coach, AI-COPILOT envelopes) MUST NOT issue PUT/POST to case-mutating endpoints.' §3 reframe row 1 states: 'AI-COPILOT envelope mode (?envelope=1): Endpoint behavior unchanged; the FRONTEND no longer auto-fires it.' These cannot both be true — if the envelope endpoint still mutates case files when invoked, then the contract is enforced at the frontend (a soft enforcement that any future caller can re-violate), not at the backend. The hard-contract framing in §2 implies backend enforcement; §3 implies frontend-only. M1.2's grep-based regression test does not resolve this, since the envelope endpoint itself is a writer.
findings.recommendation: Pick one canonical enforcement layer and state it explicitly. Two viable options: (a) backend hard-strip — envelope endpoint loses its mutation behavior in M1, returning advisory payload only (matches §2); (b) frontend-only enforcement — §2 wording is loosened to 'AI orchestration code paths shall not auto-fire the envelope's mutation mode', and §3's claim is preserved. Either is defensible; the current text is internally inconsistent.

findings.title: M1.2 grep-based regression test is brittle for a load-bearing hard contract
findings.problem: The proposed contract test 'greps services/ai_actions/ + routes/ai_* for any requests.post, client.put, api.meshImported, api.setupBC calls and fails the build if found' is the sole enforcement of the entire AI-is-advisor contract. String-matching tests are easy to evade (e.g., aliasing, dynamic dispatch, indirect import, helper extraction outside the grepped paths), produce false positives on comment/docstring matches, and miss new mutation endpoints that haven't been listed. Given this contract is the charter's deepest claim, the enforcement should be commensurate with the claim's weight.
findings.recommendation: Strengthen with at least one behavioral test: e.g., a pytest that imports the AI tool dispatcher with a sentinel HTTP client recording every outbound call and asserts the call set's verb is GET-only. Keep the grep test as a fast-pre-commit lint, but make the behavioral test the load-bearing gate. Additionally: enumerate the case-mutating endpoint list in a single registry module (e.g., MUTATING_ROUTES = {...}) so 'new mutation endpoint' is not silently outside the test's coverage.

findings.title: counter_impact justification cites a Kogami-skip clause that does not apply
findings.problem: The frontmatter says counter_impact: +1 with rationale '...Kogami: charter DECs are not code-diff reviews per project CLAUDE.md §"Skip Kogami when ... meta-DECs touching DEC-V61-087 / its successors".' But this DEC IS Kogami-triggered (the very review you're reading), per the autonomous_governance_rule_change trigger explicitly named in the same frontmatter. The 'Skip Kogami' clause referenced is for meta-Kogami-files self-modification, which the DEC itself acknowledges does not apply here ('but this DEC is NOT meta-Kogami-files'). The cited skip-rationale is therefore self-contradictory and should be removed.
findings.recommendation: Strike the 'Kogami: charter DECs are not code-diff reviews...' phrase from the counter_impact justification. The substantive point — 'Codex governance review not directly triggered because no code diff' — stands on its own and is not in dispute.

findings.title: Risk register missing a multi-month-no-external-validation risk
findings.problem: The charter commits to 22-35 sub-DECs across M2-M5 (mesh + physics + materials + BCs + solver + post) before AI advisor M6 ships. Risk #1 acknowledges 'workbench is genuinely below Fluent parity' until M2-M5 finish but mitigates only via UI labeling. There is no mitigation for the strategic risk that the project executes a multi-month feature build-out with no external validation gate (the prior ROADMAP M5-M8 had a binding stranger-dogfood completion gate; this charter does not appear to carry it forward — see P1 finding #1). If M2-M5 takes 3-6 months and at the end no engineer adopts the workbench, the AI-advisor pivot is unprovable.
findings.recommendation: Add a §6 risk #5 'long execution window with no external validation' and propose at least one interim validation milestone — e.g., 'after M3 close, one CFD-literate non-project-member runs a representative case end-to-end through the workbench-only path.' This anchors the charter's progress to engineer feedback rather than internal feature-count metrics.

findings.title: Module coverage percentages have no measurement methodology
findings.position: §2 Principle A (coverage targets) and §4 (per-M coverage deltas)
findings.problem: Targets like 'A Geometry/Import: 30% → 70%' and 'C Physics models: 5% → 50%' are quoted as if measurable but no methodology is specified for how '30%' or '70%' is computed. Without a definition, these become rhetorical numbers and the M-close acceptance criteria are not falsifiable.
findings.recommendation: Either (a) replace percentages with concrete capability checklists per module (e.g., 'M3 close = turbulence model picker supports k-ε, k-ω, SST, SA; energy equation toggle; multiphase off + VOF') and drop the percentage framing, or (b) cite a coverage-measurement source (e.g., a Fluent feature-list reference document) and define the percentage relative to it.

strategic_assessment: The charter is a substantively coherent strategic pivot: the engineer-trust diagnosis is sound, the workbench-parity-gap diagnosis is sound, and the AI-advisor-only contract (Principles A/B/C) is the right shape for industrial CFD culture. The decision-arc coherence is strong — V127/V128/V129a are correctly identified as compatible (display-only); V97/V98/V100 auto-apply paths are correctly identified as the work to deprecate. The §3 stays/deprecates/reframes tables are concrete and grep-able, which is the right register for a charter. The principal coherence weakness is unresolved interaction with the existing ROADMAP.md M-sequences (P1 finding #1) — particularly the binding M5-M8 commitments (stranger dogfood, Path-A recruitment, M5.1 trust-core micro-PR) which are mature governance commitments that this charter does not visibly account for. Roadmap fit is therefore NOT YET clean: the new M1-M6 cannot simply replace the prior arc without explicit succession of those commitments. Out-of-scope hygiene is good (charter does not propose code or re-litigate accepted DECs); risk-versus-benefit framing is reasonable but undersells the multi-month-without-validation risk.
